newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: United in grief, fathers mourn Dunblane, Port Arthur.
newsitem.headline: United in grief, fathers mourn Dunblane, Port Arthur.

text.p: Four men whose children were shot in the Dunblane and Port Arthur massacres met in Australia on Monday to share their grief and anger over guns.

Dunblane's Les Morton, John Crozier and Gordon Bounds, whose children died or were maimed in the massacre of 16 school pupils in the Scottish town more than a year ago, met Walter Mikac whose wife and two daughters died soon after at Port Arthur in Australia.

They held a joint news conference in Hobart, capital of the island state of Tasmania where disturbed young loner, Martin Bryant, shot dead 35 people among the ruins of the former convict settlement of Port Arthur last April 28.
"These were lunatics with guns," Morton said of both Bryant, 29, and Dunblane gunman Thomas Hamilton.
Hamilton shot himself dead after opening fire with pistols on grade-one pupils in a school gymnasium on March 13 last year.
Bryant, who used semi-automatic rifles in his murderous spree, has been jailed for life without parole.

"If they'd been lunatics without guns, our children might still be alive today, Walter's family might still be alive today," said Morton, whose five-year-old daughter Emily was gunned down at Dunblane.
"You cannot dissociate the person from the gun."
Riding a wave of anti-gun sentiment after the massacres, Britain and Australia tightened firearm laws. But the bereaved fathers on Monday called for more restrictions.
Crozier, whose five-year-old daughter Emma died at Dunblane, appealed to other fathers to help rid society of guns and to ensure existing gun control laws were not watered down.
"I'm just an ordinary dad, and I'd just like ordinary dads as well to speak out, write to the newspapers and to make it an issue at every available opportunity," Crozier said.
Mikac, whose wife Nanette and daughters Madeline, 3, and Alannah, 6, were shot dead by Bryant, said he felt numb as the April 28 anniversary of the Port Arthur killings approached.
"I feel a bit numb, angry, a little bit angry, that's really about as far as I've let myself go," Mikac said.
"Really, all I can think about is that I'm in a dream."
Survivors and family of the victims of the Dunblane and Port Arthur massacres have forged personal bonds over the past year, as the two small communities learn to cope with the tragedies.

The three Dunblane fathers visited Port Arthur on Sunday. They were invited here by the National Coalition for Gun Control, which said on Monday it now wanted a blanket ban on all high-calibre handguns in Australia.
"The types of handgun as used by Thomas Hamilton at Dunblane are still legally available in Australia," coalition spokesman Roland Browne told Reuters.
The Port Arthur community, on the southeast tip of Tasmania, will mark the first anniversary of the massacre with a memorial service at the site's convict-built stone church.
